=={{header|Cxc}}==

Conway's Game of Life models its state as what it actually is: a <em>set of live cells</em>. The <code>alive_cells</code> field is a sparse <code>Set of Cell</code>, not a dense bit grid — a blinker is three Cells, not twenty-five Bools. <code>alive(x:, y:)</code> is a one-line set membership test; <code>next_cell(x:, y:)</code> states the Life rule as the algebraic expression it is; <code>neighbors</code> sums eight <code>.to_int()</code> conversions; <code>row_at(y:)</code> renders a row by asking <code>alive</code> five times. The step driver lives in <code>main</code>: each tick asks Grid to start a new frame, visits every (x, y) in the grid with a single <code>|> g.step_cell(...)</code> dispatch, then commits and renders. Three generations of a blinker (horizontal → vertical → horizontal) print under this driver.

<syntaxhighlight lang="text">
def Cell:
    x: Int!
    y: Int!

def Grid:
    alive_cells: Set of Cell = [Cell(x: 1, y: 2), Cell(x: 2, y: 2), Cell(x: 3, y: 2)]
    next_alive:  Set of Cell = []
    width:       Int! = 5
    height:      Int! = 5

    alive(x: Int!, y: Int!) :- Bool!
        self.alive_cells.contains(Cell(x: x, y: y))

    neighbors(x: Int!, y: Int!) :- Int!
        self.alive(x: x - 1, y: y - 1).to_int() + self.alive(x: x, y: y - 1).to_int() + self.alive(x: x + 1, y: y - 1).to_int() + self.alive(x: x - 1, y: y).to_int() + self.alive(x: x + 1, y: y).to_int() + self.alive(x: x - 1, y: y + 1).to_int() + self.alive(x: x, y: y + 1).to_int() + self.alive(x: x + 1, y: y + 1).to_int()

    next_cell(x: Int!, y: Int!) :- Bool!
        alias a :- self.alive(x: x, y: y)
        alias n :- self.neighbors(x: x, y: y)
        n == 3 or (a and n == 2)

    row_at(y: Int!) :- String!
        alias c0 :- ||: self.alive(x: 0, y: y) : "#" |?: "."
        alias c1 :- ||: self.alive(x: 1, y: y) : "#" |?: "."
        alias c2 :- ||: self.alive(x: 2, y: y) : "#" |?: "."
        alias c3 :- ||: self.alive(x: 3, y: y) : "#" |?: "."
        alias c4 :- ||: self.alive(x: 4, y: y) : "#" |?: "."
        c0 + c1 + c2 + c3 + c4

    -> running

    running <: start_frame -> running
        then:
            next_alive => self.next_alive.empty()

    running <: step_cell(x: Int!, y: Int!):
        |: self.next_cell(x: x, y: y) -> running
            then: next_alive => self.next_alive.insert(Cell(x: x, y: y))
        |: else -> running

    running <: commit -> running
        then:
            alive_cells => self.next_alive

    running <: render -> running
        then:
            print(self.row_at(y: 0))
            print(self.row_at(y: 1))
            print(self.row_at(y: 2))
            print(self.row_at(y: 3))
            print(self.row_at(y: 4))
            print("")

def main:
    g: Grid = Grid()

    -> running
        then:
            |> g.render()
            self :> tick(gen: 0, cursor: 0)

    running <: tick(gen: Int!, cursor: Int!):
        |: gen >= 2 -> end
        |: cursor == 0 -> running
            then:
                |> g.start_frame()
                |> g.step_cell(x: 0, y: 0)
                self :> tick(gen: gen, cursor: 1)
        |: cursor >= g.width * g.height -> running
            then:
                |> g.commit()
                |> g.render()
                self :> tick(gen: gen + 1, cursor: 0)
        |: else -> running
            then:
                |> g.step_cell(x: cursor % g.width, y: cursor / g.width)
                self :> tick(gen: gen, cursor: cursor + 1)
</syntaxhighlight>

A few notes for readers coming from imperative Life implementations:

* <code>alive_cells: Set of Cell</code> is the state. The initial blinker is three Cells; no padding zeros, no grid-size encoding leak. The record <code>Cell</code> hashes and compares by value — two <code>Cell(x: 2, y: 2)</code> literals constructed at different call sites are set-equal, which is what membership needs.
* <code>width</code> and <code>height</code> are a view parameter, not state. Life's rule has no bounds; the set lives on <code>ℤ × ℤ</code>. The grid size matters only for how much of the plane the renderer scans.
* <code>alive(x, y)</code> is set membership in one line — no bounds check, no array index. Out-of-range coordinates are just coordinates not in the set.
* <code>next_cell</code> states the Life rule as its algebra: a cell is alive next tick iff <code>n == 3</code> or (<code>a</code> and <code>n == 2</code>). The three Wikipedia cases ((alive, 2), (alive, 3), (dead, 3) → alive) all reduce to this one boolean expression.
* <code>Bool.to_int()</code> maps <code>true → 1</code>, <code>false → 0</code>. Eight copies in <code>neighbors</code> sum to the live-neighbor count.
* Each <code>step</code> advances the generation through a three-message protocol on Grid: <code>start_frame</code> clears <code>next_alive</code>, <code>step_cell(x:, y:)</code> inserts into <code>next_alive</code> if the rule says so, <code>commit</code> flips <code>alive_cells ← next_alive</code>. <code>main</code> drives the (x, y) walk with its own cursor across <code>tick(gen:, cursor:)</code> because cxc forbids <code>|&gt;</code> self-sends on the same atom (spec §1.11). The cursor-driven loop in <code>main</code> is the cxc idiom when an iteration needs to visit <code>W × H</code> cells and the caller needs to wait for completion before rendering. A dedicated iteration primitive (Range, <code>Set.flat_map</code>) would collapse the loop, both deferred follow-ons.
* <code>||:</code> marks an expression-position multi-arm dispatch: the first arm whose guard holds yields its body value. The closing <code>|?:</code> arm covers the no-match case. Together they replace <code>if</code>/<code>else if</code>/<code>else</code>; cxc has no <code>if</code> expression at v1.0.
* <code>|&gt;</code> is a synchronous processing barrier — <code>g.step_cell(...)</code> completes before <code>main</code>'s next statement runs. <code>:&gt;</code> (used for <code>self :&gt; tick</code>) is async enqueue on the atom's own queue — essential here because <code>|&gt;</code> self-sends would deadlock the serial queue.
* Observation bodies treat each indented line as a separate statement. The eight-neighbor sum in <code>neighbors</code> stays on one physical line. <code>row_at</code>'s five alias lines could collapse to one <code>.map(v =&gt; …).join("")</code> pipeline if we kept a dense cells view alongside the set; the sparse-only implementation here stays honest at the cost of five aliases.
